inline.s: Having seen this, it is called seeing Amitayus, the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, and the Land of Ultimate Bliss. This is the universal contemplation, known as the twelfth contemplation. The Buddha of Immeasurable Life has countless transformation bodies, and together with Avalokitesvara and Mahasthamaprapta, he constantly comes to the place where this practicer dwells.

Thus, when this contemplation is perfected, it is called seeing the Buddha of Immeasurable Life and the Land of Ultimate Bliss. It is called the universal contemplation, known as the twelfth contemplation. The Buddha of Immeasurable Life has countless transformation bodies, and together with Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva and Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva, he constantly comes to the place where this practicer dwells.

The Buddha told Ananda and Queen Vaidehi: If one wishes to be reborn in the West with a sincere mind, one should first contemplate an image sixteen feet in height, standing upon the water of the pond. As said earlier, the body of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life is boundless, beyond the reach of the mind of ordinary beings; yet because of the power of the Tathagata's past vows, whoever recollects and contemplates him will surely succeed.

The Buddha told Ananda and Queen Vaidehi: If one wishes to be reborn in the West with a sincere mind, one should first contemplate the image of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, sixteen feet in height, standing upon the water of the pond. As said earlier, the body of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life is boundless, not within the reach of the mind of ordinary beings; yet because of the power of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life's past vows, whoever recollects and contemplates him will surely succeed.

But merely contemplating an image of the Buddha already yields immeasurable merit, how much more so contemplating the Buddha's complete body of marks! Amitabha Buddha, through his transcendent powers, transforms freely throughout the ten directions. Sometimes he manifests a great body filling the entire sky; sometimes a small body, sixteen feet or eight feet. Whatever form he manifests, it is all of true gold color, with its halo of light, its transformation Buddhas, and its jewelled lotus flowers, as described above.

Merely contemplating an image of the Buddha already yields immeasurable merit, how much more so contemplating the Buddha's complete body of marks! Amitabha Buddha, through his transcendent powers, transforms freely throughout the ten directions. Sometimes he manifests a great body filling the entire sky; sometimes a small body, sixteen feet or eight feet. Whatever form he manifests, it is all of true gold color, with its halo of light, its transformation Buddhas, and its jewelled lotus flowers, as described above.
As for the halo of light and the transformation Buddhas, these are as the earlier scripture passage said:

The halo of light of that Buddha is like a hundred billion great trichiliocosms. Within that halo of light there are a hundred million billion nayuta transformation Buddhas, as numerous as the sand of the Ganges. Each transformation Buddha likewise has many countless transformation bodhisattvas as his attendants.

Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva and Mahasthamaprapta, in all places, have bodies the same as sentient beings. But by observing only the distinguishing marks of their heads, one knows this is Avalokitesvara, and knows this is Mahasthamaprapta. These two bodhisattvas assist Amitabha Buddha in universally transforming all beings. This is the contemplation of miscellaneous forms, known as the thirteenth contemplation.

Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva and Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva, in all places, have bodies the same as sentient beings. But by observing only the distinguishing marks of the heads of these bodhisattvas, one knows this is Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva, and knows this is Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva. These two bodhisattvas assist Amitabha Buddha in universally transforming all sentient beings. The above contemplation is called the contemplation of miscellaneous forms, known as the thirteenth contemplation.

As for 'but observing only the distinguishing marks of the heads, one knows this is Avalokitesvara and knows this is Mahasthamaprapta': the crown of Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva has a standing Buddha (as the earlier scripture passage says:
Within his heavenly crown is a standing transformation Buddha.
), and the topknot of Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva has a jewelled flask (as the earlier scripture passage says:
Upon his flesh topknot is a jewelled flask, holding every kind of light, universally displaying the Buddha's works.
). By these one can distinguish whether it is Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva, and whether it is Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva.

blocks.text: 14. The Contemplation of the Highest Grade of Rebirth (the assembly of bodhisattvas)

inline.s: The following three contemplations — the highest grade of rebirth, the middle grade, and the lowest grade — contemplate the manner of rebirth of beings already reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss (the assembly of bodhisattvas, the assembly of sravakas, and the assembly of the common folk). Because this scripture contemplates the dependent and primary retributions of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, and not the beings of the Saha world. In the passage above the Buddha said:
The Tathagata now teaches Queen Vaidehi and all sentient beings of future ages to contemplate the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Within the nine grades: the three stages of the highest grade are the assembly of bodhisattvas of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss; the three stages of the middle grade are the assembly of sravakas of that land; the three stages of the lowest grade are the assembly of the common folk of that land. The three classes and nine grades gather together all the holy and ordinary beings of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Dependent and primary retributions: the dependent retribution and the primary retribution. The land, buildings, dwellings, and implements, being what the body depends upon, are called the dependent retribution; the body of sentient beings, which is a provisional union of the five aggregates, is the result of karmic actions created in the past and is called the primary retribution. The five aggregates: the aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness. These five are called aggregates because they are produced through accumulation; and because they can cover over a person's true nature, causing delusion and inversion and the creation of all kinds of karma, they are also called the five coverings. Among them, the aggregate of form refers to matter and is called form dharmas; the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness belong to the mind and are called mind dharmas. These are the five great elements that constitute body and mind. Of these, the aggregate of form is the physical body, and the other four aggregates — feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness — are the mind.
The Buddha told Ananda and Queen Vaidehi: All beings who are reborn in the West are of nine grades:
The Buddha told Ananda and Queen Vaidehi: Those who have already been reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss are altogether of nine grades.

blocks.text: (1) The Highest Stage of the Highest Grade

inline.s: As for those of the highest stage of the highest grade: if any sentient being wishes to be reborn in that land, he should develop three kinds of minds, and he will thereupon be reborn. What are these three? First, the mind of utmost sincerity; second, the deep mind; third, the mind of dedication of merit and the making of vows. Whoever is endowed with these three minds will surely be reborn in that land.

As for those of the highest stage of the highest grade: if any sentient being wishes to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, he should develop three kinds of minds, and he will thereupon be reborn. Which three? First, the mind of utmost sincerity; second, the deep mind; third, the mind of dedication of merit and the making of vows. Whoever is endowed with these three minds will surely be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.

The mind of utmost sincerity: 'utmost' means leaving no room for anything else; 'sincerity' means this single mind alone. Being resolved to seek rebirth in the Pure Land, cultivating with undivided attention without interruption — this is called utmost sincerity. The deep mind: this is the mind of deep faith. With a deep mind one believes and understands and is always self-possessed and pure.

Dedication of merit: 'turning one's own roots of goodness toward a goal' — concentrating the power of the roots of goodness one has created upon a certain objective, so that it may be realized as swiftly as possible. For example, all the various good deeds cultivated through one's three kinds of action (bodily, verbal, and mental action), and even all the merits of confession, entreaty, and so on, are dedicated to all sentient beings of the Dharma realm, that they may together realize bodhi. The Commentary on the Treatise on Rebirth says:
Dedication means turning one's own merit and offering it universally to sentient beings, that together they may see Amitabha Tathagata and be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
The verse 'Making Vows of Refuge in the Three Jewels' by Master Shandao says:
May this merit be given universally to all equally; may we together awaken the bodhi mind and be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
(from the Four-Volume Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra)

Making vows: to establish a firm vow, resolved to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. The mind of dedication and of making vows: the mind that both dedicates merit and makes vows — all roots of goodness, wholly from a mind of genuine deep faith, are dedicated to all sentient beings of the Dharma realm, and one vows to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Roots of goodness: the goodness of the three actions of body, speech, and mind, which being firmly planted cannot be uprooted — this is called root. Moreover, goodness can produce marvelous fruits and give rise to further goodness, and so it is called root.
The Lingzhi Commentary (the Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, Song
dynasty, composed by the monk Yuanzhao of Lingzhi Chongfu Monastery on West Lake) says:
'If
(these three minds)
are matched to the three gatherings
(the three-gathering pure precepts)
: the first is the observance of the rules of discipline
(the precept of observing the rules of discipline)
, cutting off all evil without exception, and so it must be utmost sincerity. The second is the gathering of wholesome dharmas
(the precept of gathering wholesome dharmas)
, cultivating every good without omission, and so it must grow ever deep. The third is the gathering of sentient beings
(the precept of gathering sentient beings)

, delivering all beings without exception, and so it must be the dedication of merit. If matched to the three Buddhas: the first is the virtue of the cessation of defilement, which is the dharmakaya Buddha; the second is the virtue of wisdom, which is the sambhogakaya Buddha; the third is the virtue of grace, which is the nirmanakaya Buddha. Since the fruit is three Buddhas, the cause must be three minds; not one may be lacking.'

The three-gathering pure precepts: the precept of observing the rules of discipline, the precept of gathering wholesome dharmas, and the precept of gathering sentient beings. The precept of observing the rules of discipline is to observe the Buddha's teachings and do no evil; the precept of gathering wholesome dharmas is to practice all good; the precept of gathering sentient beings is to cultivate all wholesome dharmas broadly so as to benefit sentient beings. The first two are self-benefit, and the third is benefiting others. Combining these two benefits for self and others is called the perfect fulfillment of the two benefits, and it is what all Mahayana scholars should uphold. The virtues of cessation, wisdom, and grace: the Buddha's three virtues of benefiting himself and others. First, the virtue of cessation — the Buddha has cut off all afflictions, is pure and unconditioned, and is free and at ease. Second, the virtue of wisdom — the Buddha's wisdom is deep and vast, knowing all things, and he is called one who knows all. Third, the virtue of grace — the Buddha's compassion is vast, and he vows to deliver all sentient beings without partiality or favoritism; among the beings of the three realms and six paths, none who has the connection fails to be delivered. Among these three virtues, wisdom and cessation belong to self-benefit, while grace belongs to benefiting others.

There are again three kinds of sentient beings who will be reborn there. What are these three? First, those with a compassionate mind who do not kill and who observe all the precepts; second, those who recite and read the Mahayana Vaipulya scriptures; third, those who cultivate the six recollections, dedicate their merit and make vows, wishing to be reborn in that Buddha land. Endowed with these merits, whether for one day or even seven days, they will be reborn there.
There are also beings who accomplish three kinds of practice (
xing

) of karmic merit who will be reborn there. Which three kinds of practice? First, a compassionate mind that does not kill, observing all the precepts; second, reciting and reading the Mahayana scriptures; third, cultivating the six recollections, dedicating merit and making vows, wishing to be reborn in that Buddha land. Whether for one day or even seven days, those who accomplish (are endowed with) the merit of these three kinds of practice will thereupon be reborn.

The three kinds of sentient beings: sentient beings who cultivate all three kinds of practice together. The Outline Commentary (the Outline Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, Qing
dynasty, by Peng Jiqing) says:

'By the three kinds of sentient beings is meant beings who cultivate the three kinds of practice together, not those who each cultivate only one. For faith and vow support each other, and understanding and practice advance each other. If even one is deficient, one cannot enter the Way.'

Practice and karmic action: the actions created by body, speech, and mind. The Devadatta chapter of the Lotus Sutra says, and the Scripture of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, spoken by the Buddha, says:
The karmic retribution of practice and action is inconceivable.
Observing all the precepts: the precepts here refer to the bodhisattva precepts. Master Shandao says:

'By observing all the precepts: if it refers to the capacities of humans, gods, and the two vehicles, it is called the lesser precepts; if it refers to persons of great mind and great practice, it is called the bodhisattva precepts. If this precept is reckoned by stage, then for those of the three stages of the upper grade it is called the bodhisattva precept.'
(from the Four-Volume Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra)

The Mahayana Vaipulya scriptures: these are the Mahayana scriptures; 'Vaipulya' scripture is a general term for the Mahayana sutras. The six recollections: first, recollection of the Buddha — recollect that the Buddha is endowed with the ten epithets, has great compassion, great pity, and great light, has measureless transcendent powers, and can pull beings out of suffering; I wish to be like the Buddha. Second, recollection of the Dharma — recollect that all the teachings spoken by the Tathagata have great merit and are the supreme wondrous medicine; I wish to realize them and give them to sentient beings. Third, recollection of the Sangha — recollect that the Sangha are disciples of the Tathagata, have attained the undefiled Dharma, are fully endowed with precepts, meditation, and wisdom, and are the field of merit for the world; I too wish to cultivate the practice of the Sangha. Fourth, recollection of the precepts — recollect that observance of the precepts has great power and can guard against all evil; I wish to uphold the precepts with vigor. Fifth, recollection of giving — recollect that giving has great merit, that it can both relieve others' suffering and remove one's own stinginess and greed; I wish to benefit all sentient beings universally through giving. Sixth, recollection of the heavens — recollect that the heavens have natural happiness, all owing to the cause of diligently cultivating the ten wholesome actions in the past; I too wish to cultivate wholesome karma diligently, so that wholesome causes may bring wholesome fruits.
Being endowed with these merits for one day or even seven days: for one day or even seven days, accomplishing the merit of these three kinds of practice

one day or even seven days) — one day or even seven days is an illustrative expression, an abbreviated way of speaking. To state it in detail, for example as the World-Honored One said in the Great Mindfulness Foundation Sutra:
'Monks! Anyone who, in this manner, correctly cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness for seven years may expect one of two fruits: in this very life attaining supreme wisdom
(realizing the fruit of arhatship)
, or, if the five aggregates remain, attaining the fruit of non-returning
(realizing the fruit of anagami)
. Monks! Not to speak of seven years,
Monks! Not to speak of six years,
Monks! Not to speak of one year,
Monks! Not to speak of seven months,
Monks! Not to speak of one month,

Monks! Not to speak of half a month; if anyone, in this manner, correctly cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness for seven days, he may expect one of two fruits: in this very life attaining supreme wisdom, or, if the five aggregates remain, attaining the fruit of non-returning.'

The four fruits: in cultivating the four noble truths there are four fruits: the fruit of stream-enterer, the fruit of once-returner, the fruit of non-returner, and the fruit of arhat. Among them, the fourth fruit, the arhat, is the highest; one who attains this fruit is released from birth and death and no longer undergoes a future existence.

When he is reborn in that land, because this person is vigorous and courageous, Amitabha Tathagata, together with Avalokitesvara, Mahasthamaprapta, countless transformation Buddhas, hundreds and thousands of monks, the great assembly of sravakas, measureless gods, and palaces of the seven treasures — with Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva holding the adamant throne and Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva — come before the practicer.

When he is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, because this person is vigorous and courageous, Amitabha Buddha, together with Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva, Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva, countless transformation Buddhas, hundreds and thousands of monks, the great assembly of sravakas, measureless gods, and palaces of the seven treasures — with Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva holding the adamant throne and Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva — come before the practicer.

Amitabha Buddha emits a great light of illumination, shining upon the practicer's body, and together with the various bodhisattvas extends his hand to welcome him. Avalokitesvara, Mahasthamaprapta, and countless bodhisattvas praise the practicer and encourage his mind.

Amitabha Buddha emits a great light of illumination, shining upon the practicer's body, and together with the various bodhisattvas extends his hand to welcome him. Avalokitesvara, Mahasthamaprapta, and countless bodhisattvas praise the practicer and encourage his mind.

When the practicer sees this, he rejoices and leaps with joy. He sees his own body riding the adamant throne, following behind the Buddha, and in the twinkling of an eye he is reborn in that land. Once reborn there, he sees the Buddha's physical body endowed with all the marks, and sees the various bodhisattvas endowed with all their marks; the light and the jeweled grove proclaim the wondrous Dharma. Upon hearing it, he immediately realizes the patient endurance of the unproduced, and in a moment he passes before the Buddhas throughout the ten directions, and before each Buddha in turn receives the prophecy of his future Buddhahood. Returning to that land, he attains measureless, hundreds and thousands of gates of dharani. This is called one of the highest stage of the highest grade.

When the practicer sees this, he rejoices and leaps with joy. He sees his own body riding the adamant throne, following behind Amitabha Buddha, and in the twinkling of an eye he is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Once reborn there, he sees the Buddha's physical body endowed with all the marks, and sees the various bodhisattvas endowed with all their marks; the light and the jeweled grove proclaim the wondrous Dharma. Upon hearing this wondrous Dharma, he immediately realizes the patient endurance of the unproduced, and in a moment he passes before the Buddhas throughout the ten directions, and before each Buddha in turn receives the prophecy. Returning to that land, he attains measureless, hundreds and thousands of gates of dharani. This is called one of the highest stage of the highest grade.
The adamant throne: a throne made of adamant. A moment (
yu

): an instant; a moment. The prophecy: receiving from the Buddha the prediction that one will in the future certainly become a Buddha. The gates of dharani: dharani, in Chinese translation, means 'to hold and maintain.' Through the method of holding and maintaining, the bodhisattva accommodates the speech and sounds of all sentient beings, guides them in right faith, causes them to extinguish all evil thoughts, and to practice all wholesome dharmas — this is called the bodhisattva's gates of dharani.
